    33→## Files Constrained by This Decision
    34→
    35→- `FieldIndex.java` — operates on DET/OPE ciphertexts for equality/range queries
    36→- `VectorFieldIndex.java` — operates on DCPE encrypted vectors for ANN
    37→- `IndexRegistry.java` — validates EncryptionSpec × index compatibility at construction

    40→
    41→## Problem
    42→How should secondary indices and queries adapt when field values are encrypted — which index types work with which EncryptionSpec variants, and what query operations are supported?
    43→
    44→## Constraints That Drove This Decision
    45→- **Correctness over capability**: better to prohibit an index than to allow one that returns wrong results — incompatible combinations must fail at schema construction, not at query time
    46→- **EncryptionSpec determines capability**: the sealed interface categorizes encryption families; index capability maps directly from scheme properties
    47→- **Fit with existing index infrastructure**: FieldIndex, VectorFieldIndex, IndexRegistry, QueryExecutor must adapt without restructuring
    48→
    49→## Decision
    50→**Chosen approach: Static Capability Matrix with Tiered Full-Text Search**
    51→
    52→Each `EncryptionSpec` variant exposes capability methods (`supportsEquality()`, `supportsRange()`, `supportsKeywordSearch()`, `supportsPhraseSearch()`, `supportsSseSearch()`, `supportsANN()`). `IndexRegistry` validates field encryption × index compatibility at schema construction time — incompatible combinations throw `IllegalArgumentException`. Existing indices operate directly on encrypted values (DET ciphertexts for equality, OPE ciphertexts for range, DCPE vectors for ANN). Full-text search on encrypted fields is supported through three tiers, all included in scope.
    53→
    54→### Capability Matrix
    55→
    56→| EncryptionSpec     | Equality | Range | Keyword | Phrase | SSE Boolean | ANN   |
    57→|--------------------|----------|-------|---------|--------|-------------|-------|
    58→| None               |    ✓     |   ✓   |    ✓    |   ✓    |      ✓      |   ✓   |
    59→| Deterministic      |    ✓     |   ✗   |  T1 ✓   |  T2 ✓  |    T3 ✓     |   ✗   |
    60→| OrderPreserving    |    ✓     |   ✓   |    ✗    |   ✗    |      ✗      |   ✗   |
    61→| DistancePreserving |    ✗     |   ✗   |    ✗    |   ✗    |      ✗      | ✓(≈)  |
    62→| Opaque             |    ✗     |   ✗   |    ✗    |   ✗    |      ✗      |   ✗   |
    63→
    64→### Full-Text Search Tiers
    65→
    66→**Tier 1 — DET keyword match (~50 lines)**
    67→Tokenize text, encrypt each term with AES-SIV (deterministic), store encrypted terms in the existing `LsmInvertedIndex` composite key format. Search: encrypt query term with same key, standard index lookup. Supports exact keyword match and boolean AND/OR.
    68→
    69→**Tier 2 — DET + OPE positions (~200 lines)**
    70→Extend inverted index postings to include OPE-encrypted term positions. Phrase query: encrypt query terms (DET), look up postings, check that OPE-encrypted positions are consecutive. Proximity: check position difference ≤ threshold on OPE ciphertexts. OPE is only used for the small position domain (integers), minimal security tradeoff.
    71→
    72→**Tier 3 — SSE encrypted inverted index (~500-800 lines)**
    73→Separate encrypted index structure per Curtmola SSE-2 / Dyn2Lev scheme. For each term, derive search token `Tw = PRF(K, term)`, encrypt document ID list under `Tw`, store in dictionary keyed by `hash(Tw)`. Minimal access-pattern leakage. Dynamic SSE supports add/delete with forward privacy. Supports keyword and boolean queries with stronger security than T1/T2.
    74→
    75→## Rationale
    76→
    77→### Why Static Capability Matrix
    78→- **Correctness**: fail-fast at schema construction — impossible to create an incompatible index/encryption combination that silently returns wrong results
    79→- **Scale**: zero runtime overhead — existing indices operate on encrypted values directly, the encryption scheme guarantees the index operation works on ciphertext
    80→- **Fit**: capability methods on the sealed EncryptionSpec interface — no new classes needed for FieldIndex or VectorFieldIndex. IndexRegistry checks before building.
    81→
    82→### Why not Encrypted Index Adapters
    83→- **Fit**: SecondaryIndex is sealed — adapters break the hierarchy or require delegation wrappers. N×M adapter classes (encryption specs × index types) to maintain. Validation at query time instead of construction.
    84→
    85→### Why not No Index on Encrypted Fields
    86→- **Disqualified**: contradicts acceptance criterion #4 ("at least one field type supports indexed search while encrypted"). Full scan at millions of QPS is prohibitive.
    87→
    88→## Implementation Guidance
    89→
    90→### EncryptionSpec capability methods
    91→From [`searchable-encryption-schemes.md#implementation-notes`](../../.kb/algorithms/encryption/searchable-encryption-schemes.md#implementation-notes):
    92→
    93→```java
    94→public sealed interface EncryptionSpec {
    95→    default boolean supportsEquality()      { return false; }
    96→    default boolean supportsRange()         { return false; }
    97→    default boolean supportsKeywordSearch() { return false; }
    98→    default boolean supportsPhraseSearch()  { return false; }
    99→    default boolean supportsSseSearch()     { return false; }
   100→    default boolean supportsANN()           { return false; }
   101→
   102→    record None() implements EncryptionSpec {
   103→        @Override public boolean supportsEquality()      { return true; }
   104→        @Override public boolean supportsRange()         { return true; }
   105→        @Override public boolean supportsKeywordSearch() { return true; }
   106→        @Override public boolean supportsPhraseSearch()  { return true; }
   107→        @Override public boolean supportsSseSearch()     { return true; }
   108→        @Override public boolean supportsANN()           { return true; }
   109→    }
   110→    record Deterministic() implements EncryptionSpec {
   111→        @Override public boolean supportsEquality()      { return true; }
   112→        @Override public boolean supportsKeywordSearch() { return true; }
   113→        @Override public boolean supportsPhraseSearch()  { return true; }
   114→        @Override public boolean supportsSseSearch()     { return true; }
   115→    }
   116→    record OrderPreserving() implements EncryptionSpec {
   117→        @Override public boolean supportsEquality()      { return true; }
   118→        @Override public boolean supportsRange()         { return true; }
   119→    }

   121→        @Override public boolean supportsANN()           { return true; }

   128→```java
   129→// In IndexRegistry, at index creation time:
   130→if (indexDef.type() == IndexType.SECONDARY && !encryption.supportsEquality()) {
   131→    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Field '" + field + "' with " +
   132→        encryption + " encryption does not support secondary index");

   136→### How indices work on encrypted values
   137→- **DET + FieldIndex**: same ciphertext for same plaintext → standard B-tree/skip-list equality works on ciphertext bytes
   138→- **OPE + FieldIndex**: ciphertext ordering preserved → range scan on ciphertext bytes works correctly
   139→- **DCPE + VectorFieldIndex**: approximate distance preserved → HNSW/IVF graph search on encrypted float[] works with degraded recall
   140→- **DET + LsmInvertedIndex (T1)**: encrypt terms before indexing, encrypt query term before lookup — standard inverted index mechanics
   141→- **DET+OPE + positional index (T2)**: terms encrypted with DET, positions with OPE — phrase check via position comparison on OPE ciphertexts
   142→- **SSE index (T3)**: separate structure — encrypted posting lists keyed by PRF-derived tokens

   144→Known edge cases from [`searchable-encryption-schemes.md#edge-cases-and-gotchas`](../../.kb/algorithms/encryption/searchable-encryption-schemes.md#edge-cases-and-gotchas):
   145→- DET leaks frequency through index — document as security tradeoff
   146→- OPE on positions leaks relative ordering — acceptable for small position domain
   147→- DCPE recall degrades with perturbation strength — tunable parameter
   148→

   150→- Prefix/wildcard queries on encrypted text (would need character-level encryption)
   151→- Fuzzy matching on encrypted text (edit distance doesn't work on ciphertexts)
   152→- Cross-field joins on encrypted values from different tables
   153→- Access-pattern leakage in T1/T2 (T3 provides stronger protection)

   157→- A new EncryptionSpec variant is added that doesn't fit the capability matrix pattern

   159→- T3 SSE performance is insufficient at scale (may need algorithmic optimization)
   160→- Forward/backward privacy requirements tighten beyond what Dyn2Lev provides

    32→## Files Constrained by This Decision
    33→
    34→- `FieldDefinition.java` — extended from `record(name, type)` to `record(name, type, encryptionSpec)`
    35→- `JlsmSchema.java` — builder gains `.field(name, type, encryptionSpec)` overloads
    36→- `DocumentSerializer.java` — dispatch table incorporates encrypt/decrypt per-field
    37→- `FieldType.java` — unchanged (encryption is orthogonal to field type)
    38→
    39→## Problem
    40→How should field-level encryption be expressed in JlsmSchema, how should keys bind to fields, and how should DocumentSerializer integrate encryption/decryption into its serialize/deserialize path?
    41→
    42→## Constraints That Drove This Decision
    43→- **Fit with existing type system**: must compose with sealed FieldType hierarchy, FieldDefinition record, JlsmSchema builder, DocumentSerializer dispatch table, and secondary indices without breaking the unencrypted API
    44→- **Type-aware encryption**: different FieldTypes need different encryption schemes — the API must express this per-field with compile-time type safety
    45→- **Scale + latency**: encryption dispatch at millions of QPS must be resolvable at schema-construction time, not per-document
    46→
    47→## Decision
    48→**Chosen approach: Schema Annotation (FieldDefinition carries EncryptionSpec)**
    49→
    50→Extend `FieldDefinition` to carry an optional `EncryptionSpec` — a sealed interface whose permits match the encryption families researched in the KB. Encryption configuration is expressed in the schema, keys are held separately in an Arena-backed `EncryptionKeyHolder`, and DocumentSerializer builds per-field encrypt/decrypt functions at construction time using the same dispatch table pattern already in use.
    51→
    52→## Rationale
    53→
    54→### Why Schema Annotation
    55→- **Fit**: FieldDefinition is a record — adding a third component with a default (`EncryptionSpec.NONE`) is natural and backward-compatible. The sealed FieldType hierarchy is untouched. DocumentSerializer's existing dispatch table pattern (just optimized) accommodates encrypt/decrypt steps trivially.
    56→- **Scale**: encryption dispatch is resolved at schema construction, not per-document. The dispatch table is built once and reused for every serialize/deserialize call — zero per-document overhead beyond the crypto operations.
    57→- **Accuracy**: `EncryptionSpec` is a sealed interface — the compiler enforces exhaustive handling. Each variant maps to a specific encryption family, preventing misconfiguration (e.g., DCPE on a boolean field).
    58→
    59→### Why not Encrypted FieldType Variants
    60→- **Fit**: expanding the sealed FieldType permits list means every `switch(type)` across DocumentSerializer, QueryExecutor, FieldIndex, SqlTranslator, and all encode/decode methods needs new arms. Encryption is a cross-cutting storage concern, not a data type property.
    61→
    62→### Why not Pluggable FieldEncryptor Interface
    63→- **Fit**: encryption becomes invisible to the schema — secondary indices can't adapt behavior, schema serialization doesn't capture it. Map lookup per field per document adds overhead at scale. No compile-time safety against misconfiguration.
    64→

    66→
    67→### EncryptionSpec sealed interface
    68→
    69→```java
    70→public sealed interface EncryptionSpec permits
    71→        EncryptionSpec.None,
    72→        EncryptionSpec.Deterministic,
    73→        EncryptionSpec.OrderPreserving,
    74→        EncryptionSpec.DistancePreserving,
    75→        EncryptionSpec.Opaque {
    76→
    77→    record None() implements EncryptionSpec {}
    78→    record Deterministic() implements EncryptionSpec {}      // AES-SIV
    79→    record OrderPreserving() implements EncryptionSpec {}     // Boldyreva OPE
    80→    record DistancePreserving() implements EncryptionSpec {}  // DCPE/SAP
    81→    record Opaque() implements EncryptionSpec {}              // AES-GCM
    82→
    83→    EncryptionSpec NONE = new None();
    84→
    85→    static EncryptionSpec none() { return NONE; }
    86→    static EncryptionSpec deterministic() { return new Deterministic(); }
    87→    static EncryptionSpec orderPreserving() { return new OrderPreserving(); }
    88→    static EncryptionSpec distancePreserving() { return new DistancePreserving(); }
    89→    static EncryptionSpec opaque() { return new Opaque(); }
    90→}
    91→```
    92→
    93→### FieldDefinition extension
    94→
    95→```java
    96→public record FieldDefinition(String name, FieldType type, EncryptionSpec encryption) {
    97→    public FieldDefinition(String name, FieldType type) {
    98→        this(name, type, EncryptionSpec.NONE);
    99→    }
   100→}
   101→```
   102→
   103→### Schema builder usage
   104→
   105→```java
   106→JlsmSchema schema = JlsmSchema.builder("users", 1)
   107→    .field("id", FieldType.Primitive.INT64)                                          // unencrypted
   108→    .field("email", FieldType.Primitive.STRING, EncryptionSpec.deterministic())       // equality search
   109→    .field("salary", FieldType.Primitive.INT64, EncryptionSpec.orderPreserving())     // range queries
   110→    .field("embedding", FieldType.vector(FLOAT32, 128), EncryptionSpec.distancePreserving()) // ANN
   111→    .field("ssn", FieldType.Primitive.STRING, EncryptionSpec.opaque())                // no search
   112→    .build();
   113→```
   114→
   115→### Key handling (from [`jvm-key-handling-patterns.md#algorithm-steps`](../../.kb/systems/security/jvm-key-handling-patterns.md#algorithm-steps))
   116→- Keys held in `EncryptionKeyHolder` using confined/shared `Arena` (off-heap)
   117→- Caller passes `byte[]` key material to table builder — library zeros the input after import
   118→- One key per table initially; per-field keys can be added as `EncryptionSpec` parameters later
   119→
   120→### DocumentSerializer integration
   121→- At `SchemaSerializer` construction, for each field with `encryption != NONE`, build a `FieldEncryptor` lambda in the dispatch table (same pattern as `FieldDecoder`)
   122→- `serialize()`: encode field value, then encrypt the encoded bytes
   123→- `deserialize()`: decrypt the encrypted bytes, then decode the field value
   124→- `EncryptionSpec.NONE` fields skip encrypt/decrypt entirely — zero overhead
   125→
   126→Known edge cases from [`searchable-encryption-schemes.md#edge-cases-and-gotchas`](../../.kb/algorithms/encryption/searchable-encryption-schemes.md#edge-cases-and-gotchas):
   127→- DET leaks frequency — document as a security tradeoff
   128→- OPE leaks approximate value — not suitable for high-sensitivity numeric fields
   129→- DCPE recall degrades with stronger perturbation — tunable tradeoff
   130→

   132→- Key rotation — requires rebuilding the table with new keys (documented limitation)
   133→- Encryption of WAL entries — separate concern, can layer on later
   134→- Schema migration from unencrypted to encrypted — requires data rewrite
   135→- Per-field key binding — initial implementation uses one key per table

   142→- Performance benchmarks show the dispatch table overhead is measurable at target QPS
